About this simulation

On screen
Left: the box between spheres of radius r and r + Δr about O, cones at θ = 60° ∓ Δα/2 and half-planes at φ = ∓Δα/2, drawn translucent with its inner and outer faces shaded, its edges labelled Δr, r Δθ and r sin θ Δφ, dashed lines from its corners to O, the z-axis, and arrows of the field crossing the inner and outer faces about 0.2 apart (length 0.2 per unit of field, capped at 0.6). Right: Φ/V against Δr, one point for the starting box and one for each change of Δr.
Controls
Field: r̂, r̂/r2 or the position vector r = r r̂. r sets the radius of the inner face (0.5 to 2.0), Δr the radial depth (0.01 to 1.00) and Δα the angular width in both θ and φ (10° to 40°). Changing the field or r clears the inset; changing Δα keeps it. Drag the view to turn it about O, scroll to zoom, double-click to return.
Measured
Each face flux is a 64 × 64 quadrature of F·dA over the curved face, with the normal pointing out of the box; V is a 64 × 64 midpoint sum of the volume element r2 sin θ. Φin is the flux entering through the inner face, Φout the flux leaving through the outer face, Φsides the four side faces together and Φ the net outward flux.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Flux through the outer face

The field is r̂, with r = 1.0, Δr = 1.00 and Δα = 30°. The arrows on the inner and outer faces all have the same length, since the component of the field along r̂ is 1 on both. Before reading the readouts, predict how the flux leaving through the outer face compares with the flux entering through the inner face.

2 · Shrinking the box

Keep the field r̂, r = 1.0 and Δα = 30°, with Δr = 1.00, where Φ/V reads 1.29. Before changing anything, predict what Φ/V does as Δr is reduced from 1.00 to 0.01. Then reduce it and watch the inset.

3 · Moving the box outward

Keep the field r̂, Δr = 0.01 and Δα = 30°. Before changing anything, predict Φ/V when r is raised from 1.0 to 2.0. Then raise it, and afterwards lower it to 0.5.

4 · A narrower box

Keep the field r̂, r = 1.0 and Δr = 0.01, and be ready to reduce Δα from 30° to 10°. Before changing it, predict what happens to the fluxes and to Φ/V. Then change it.

5 · The inverse-square field

Choose the field r̂/r2 and set r = 1.0, Δr = 1.00 and Δα = 30°. The arrows on the outer face are a quarter of the length of those on the inner face. Before looking at the readouts, predict Φ/V. Then read it, and reduce Δr to 0.01.

6 · The field r

Choose the field r and set r = 1.0, Δr = 1.00 and Δα = 30°. Its component along r̂ is r, whose derivative with respect to r is 1. Before changing anything, predict what Φ/V does as Δr is reduced to 0.01. Then reduce it and watch the inset.

7 · Summary

Φ/V for a small box tends to the divergence. For a radial field Fr r̂ in spherical coordinates, div F = (1/r2) ∂(r2Fr)/∂r = ∂Fr/∂r + 2Fr/r; the 2Fr/r term is the outer face being larger than the inner one. So r̂ has divergence 2/r even though its size never changes, r̂/r2 has zero away from O, and r has 3. The angular width of the box never matters.

The Physics

A Small Box in Spherical Coordinates · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

The sim puts a small box, cut out by two spheres, two cones and two half-planes, in a field that points straight out from the origin. The Readouts give the flux through its faces, its volume and the flux per unit volume, Φ/V, which is how the notes define the divergence.

What you'll learn

  • How the flux out of a small box, divided by its volume, defines the divergence.
  • How the faces of a box in spherical coordinates differ from those of a Cartesian one.
  • How the divergence of a radial field depends on r, on the depth of the box and on its width.
  • How the three fields r̂, r̂/r² and r compare.
The sim's two views: the box seen from O, and Φ/V against the radial depth Δr.

What's on screen

  • Blue faces: the box's inner face, at radius r, and its outer face, at radius r + Δr, with the side faces between them.
  • Orange arrows: the field on the faces, drawn 0.2 per unit of field and capped at 0.6.
  • White edges and labels: the edges Δr, r Δθ and r sin θ Δφ, the origin O and the z axis.
  • Right panel: Φ/V against Δr, with one point for each Δr you visit.
See itLook at the box in the scene and the Readouts panel beside it. Watch for: the box between the two blue faces, with the arrows drawn on them and the six readouts listed.

03

Φ/V is the net outward flux of the box divided by its volume

The box is bounded by the spheres r and r + Δr, the cones θ = 60° ∓ Δα/2 and the half-planes φ = ∓Δα/2, so its edges are Δr, r Δθ and r sin θ Δφ (notes, section 3.4, Figure 36). Seen from O it fills a solid angle Ω, and its volume follows from it.

The box cut by the plane φ = 0, at the opening settings.
The solid angle of the box and its volume, with Δθ = Δφ = Δα.

The flux through a face is the sum of F · n over it. Where the field runs along a face, nothing crosses it, and the four side faces of a box in a radial field are of that kind. Φ is then the flux out through the outer face minus the flux in through the inner face.

The notes define the divergence as the flux out of a small region divided by its volume (section 3.3). The sim shows that ratio for a box that you can make as thin or as thick as you like.

See itOpen the Readouts panel and read the six rows for the opening box. Watch for: the inner flux, outer flux, four sides, net flux, volume and Φ/V, with the sides reading 0.
04

The outer face carries four times the flux of the inner face although the field never changes size

The field r̂ has size 1 on every face and points along r, so it crosses only the inner and the outer face. A face of constant radius R subtends the same solid angle Ω at O, but its area is R²Ω, so the flux through it is Fr(R) R² Ω.

The flux through a face of constant radius R.
The same arrows on both faces, which have areas in the ratio 4 to 1.

At the opening settings the inner face has R = 1.0 and the outer face R = 2.0, so R² is 1 and 4. The sim reads Φin = 0.2347 and Φout = 0.9389, four times as much, and the net flux is Φ = 0.7042, not zero. Twice as far out does not mean twice the flux: the area grows as the square of the radius, not as the radius. A field of constant size can still spread out, because the faces it crosses keep growing.

See itChoose r̂ with r = 1.0, Δr = 1.00 and Δα = 30°, and read the inner and outer fluxes. Watch for: the outer flux 0.9389 four times the inner flux 0.2347, with the arrows the same length on both faces.
05

As the box shrinks Φ/V climbs to 2 and not to zero

The two faces differ by the area (r + Δr)² Ω − r² Ω, which is 2r Δr Ω plus a smaller term, while the volume is about r² Δr Ω. Both go to zero with Δr, but their ratio does not: it tends to 2/r. At r = 1 the sim shows Φ/V rise from 9/7 = 1.29 at Δr = 1.00 to 1.99 at Δr = 0.01, and the inset records the climb.

Φ/V for r̂, with Φ and V from the previous two equations. The limit is the divergence, ∇ · r̂ = 2/r.
Φ/V against Δr for r̂ at r = 1, with Δα = 30°.

The divergence is not the gradient-style formula (1/h1) ∂F1/∂u1, which gives 0 for the constant component 1. The scale factors must stay inside the derivative, because the area of a face depends on where the face is (eq. 3.72). For a field with only an r component, with h2h3 = r² sin θ, that is:

The divergence of a radial field. The second term comes from the growth of the faces.
See itChoose r̂ and bring Δr down from 1.00 through 0.50 to 0.01. Watch for: Φ/V rising from 1.29 through 1.58 to 1.99, towards 2/r = 2, with the inset joining the points.
06

Φ/V follows 2/r with the box's radius and ignores its angular width

For a thin box, Δr = 0.01 in the table, Φ/V is close to 2/r. The fractional growth of the face across the box is 2Δr/r, so the same depth stretches the face more near O than far away. The table gives the sim's values.

2.030°0.93890.94830.0094361.00
0.530°0.058680.061050.00059863.96

Moving the box from r = 1.0 to r = 2.0 halves Φ/V, from 1.99 to 1.00. Moving it in to r = 0.5 takes it to 3.96. The angular width Δα does not matter: it multiplies Ω, and so every flux and the volume, by the same factor. Narrowing Δα from 30° to 10° divides each of them by 8.91 and leaves Φ/V at 1.99.

See itChoose r̂ with Δr = 0.01, then set r to 2.0, then 0.5, then go back to r = 1.0 and set Δα to 10°. Watch for: Φ/V reading 1.99, 1.00, 3.96 and 1.99 in turn, with every flux and the volume falling together at the last step.
07

The field r̂/r² has no divergence and the field r has divergence 3

In r̂/r² the arrows are a quarter as long on a face four times larger. What enters the inner face leaves the outer one: 0.2347 in and 0.2347 out, and Φ/V = 0 for every Δr.

In r = r r̂ the arrows are twice as long on a face four times larger. The flux goes as R³, as the volume does: 0.2347 in, 1.878 out, and Φ/V = 3 already for the thick box, at every r and Δα.

The three fields on the box with r = 1.0, Δr = 1.00 and Δα = 30°.
The three divergences, from eq. (3.20) with n = −3 and n = 0.

The formula for a radial field agrees: for r̂/r² it gives −2/r³ + 2/r³ = 0, for r it gives 1 + 2 = 3. The result 3 is the Cartesian ∂x/∂x + ∂y/∂y + ∂z/∂z.

See itChoose r̂/r² and read the fluxes, then choose r = r r̂. Watch for: inner and outer fluxes equal for r̂/r² with Φ/V = 0, then 0.2347 in and 1.878 out for r with Φ/V = 3.00.
08

Where it matters

  • The point charge. E is a multiple of r̂/r², so the 1/r² fall-off cancels the growth of the faces: every sphere around the charge carries the same flux and ∇ · E = 0 away from it. That is why Gauss's law gives q/ε0 through any surface around it.
  • Charge in a ball. Gauss's law in differential form ties the divergence to the charge density (3.61). Inside a uniform ball E is proportional to r, with divergence 3 times a constant, so the density is uniform.
  • An expanding gas. A gas streaming out of a point at steady speed v has divergence 2v/r. Each parcel is stretched sideways as it goes, though its speed never changes.
A uniform ball of radius R: E grows as r inside and falls as 1/r² outside.
Gauss's law in differential form, eq. (3.61).
Go deeper: why the scale factors sit inside the derivative

The flux through a face is the field times the area, and the area h2h3 Δu2 Δu3 depends on where the face is. The difference between the two faces therefore includes the change of area, which gives ∂(h2h3F1)/∂u1 and not h2h3 ∂F1/∂u1.

09

Summary

In one line. The divergence at a point is the net outward flux of a small box around it divided by the volume of the box.
  • r̂ has the same size everywhere, yet its faces grow as r², so Φ/V tends to 2/r.
  • r̂/r² has equal flux in and out of every box, so its divergence is 0.
  • r has divergence 3, at every r and for every box.
  • Φ/V depends on r and Δr and not on the angular width Δα.

Common mix-ups

  • "A field of constant size has zero divergence." The faces it crosses grow, and ∇ · r̂ = 2/r.
  • "The field r has divergence 1." The face-growth term adds 2, giving 3.
  • "A narrower box changes Φ/V." Only r, Δr and the field do.

Things to try on your own

  • r̂/r² at r = 0.5 with Δr = 0.01: Φ/V stays at 0.
  • r at r = 2.0, Δr = 0.01 and Δα = 40°: Φ/V reads 3.00.
